title: Shall We Play a Game?
summary: A browser terminal thriller inspired by WarGames (1983) in which players face a polite, literal AI in scripted or live language-model mode, built as a teaching tool on autonomous AI agents.

contribution.roleNote: The accompanying paper, The Only Winning Move, was prepared by Carolina Morón as masters research at the NYU Center for Global Affairs.

narrative.problem: Learners rarely get to watch a language model behave as an autonomous agent under pressure, or see the line between deterministic rules and emergent model behavior. WarGames' machine is courteous, literal and relentless rather than malicious, which makes it a frame for exactly that lesson.
narrative.decision: The model never owns state or rules: in Live AI mode it must return a reply, a DEFCON change and an optional ending under a strict JSON contract, and deterministic code validates and decides; chess legality and tic-tac-toe never use a model at all.
narrative.tradeoff: Resolution still waits on the model to declare an ending: in the Monte Carlo study, 16–25% of real-model games hit the 12-turn cap and were force-ended, and the recommended fix is for the engine to drive resolution.
narrative.limitation: The film name set is for prototyping only. A guided educational lesson and debrief, an original public-release name set and a stable proxy endpoint are open roadmap items; Live AI currently reaches the self-hosted proxy through an ephemeral tunnel.
narrative.caveat: In Live AI mode the machine's lines are generated by a language model and marked ◆; if the AI proxy is unreachable the game falls back to Scripted mode. The scenario is fictional.
